\chapter{More of the Kitchen --- Pan, Oven, Fork, Garlic, Soup}
\label{ch:la-cocina}
\hlchaptermodality{297}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name the pan, the oven, the fork, the garlic and the soup in Spanish, and thank somebody for the meal.}

Complete ES-C297-sopa: name all five of the kitchen in order and thank somebody for what came out of it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[la sartén]{la sartén — the accent that is a receipt}

\label{lesson:ES-C297-sarten}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what does \emph{un gallina} call somebody? (A coward.) And what did \emph{burrus} mean? (Reddish.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la olla — the deep one you already have.
  \item el plato — where the food ends up.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sar-TÉN}, stress on the very end, which is what the written accent is telling you. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la sartén} — \textquotedblleft{}the frying pan,\textquotedblright{} the shallow one you fry in.

Latin \textbf{sartago} was already exactly that, and the Romans already fried in it. The word came down through the sideways form \emph{sartaginem}, which is where the \emph{-n} on the end comes from.

The accent is the part worth stopping on. Spanish only writes one when the stress falls somewhere the default rules would not put it, so an accent is never decoration — it is a receipt. A word ending in \emph{-n} is expected to be stressed on the part before last. \emph{Sartén} is not, so it must say so.

Now make it plural and watch the receipt get handed back: \emph{sartenes} ends in \emph{-s} and is stressed on the part before last, which is exactly what the rules already predict. No accent needed, so no accent written. The mark did not move; the reason for it disappeared.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A pan, and a small piece of proof that the accents are not arbitrary.

If you can say why \emph{sartén} wears one and \emph{sartenes} does not, you can predict the mark on most words you meet rather than memorising it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la sartén}
  \item \emph{la sartén}, then \emph{las sartenes} — hear the stress stay put
  \item \emph{la olla}, then \emph{la sartén}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{sartago}? (A frying pan.) Why does \emph{sartén} wear an accent? (Because the stress is final and a word ending in \emph{-n} would not be.) And why does \emph{sartenes} not? (The rules already predict its stress.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el horno]{el horno — an f buried under an h}

\label{lesson:ES-C297-horno}



\begin{quote}
Two back: what is a \emph{burrito}, taken literally? (A little donkey.) And why does \emph{sartén} carry an accent? (Its stress is final, against the rule.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item f $\to$ h — the change this word is a specimen of.
  \item la sartén — the shallow one, from just before.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{OR-no}, stress on the first part. The \emph{h} is written and not said, which is the whole point of it. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el horno} — \textquotedblleft{}the oven.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{furnus}, an oven or a bakehouse. You already know what happened to the \emph{f-}: it thinned to a breathy sound, the breath faded, and Spanish went on writing the letter over the empty space. \emph{Furnus} to \emph{forno} to \emph{horno}.

So the \emph{h} is a headstone. Say \emph{OR-no} and you are saying the word correctly; the letter is there to tell you what used to be.

English took the same Latin word later and by a different door, straight out of the books, so it never got worn down: a \textbf{furnace} still has its \emph{f}, and so does the older sense of \textbf{furnish} — to supply, as a bakehouse supplies bread.

One more thing you can now do. Meet an unfamiliar Spanish word beginning with a silent \emph{h}, put an \emph{f} back on the front, and see whether a Latin or English word falls out. It works often enough to be worth trying every time.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of the kitchen, and a decoder you can run on strangers.

\emph{La sartén} explained a mark you can see. \emph{El horno} explains a letter you cannot hear. Both are the same lesson: written Spanish keeps records, and the records are readable.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el horno}
  \item \emph{la sartén}, then \emph{el horno}
  \item \emph{el pan del horno}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{furnus}? (An oven.) What is the \emph{h} in \emph{horno} marking? (An \emph{f} that wore away.) And which English word kept the \emph{f}? (\emph{Furnace}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el tenedor]{el tenedor — a word you can build yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C297-tenedor}



\begin{quote}
What was \emph{sartago}? (A frying pan.) And what letter is hiding under the \emph{h} of \emph{horno}? (An \emph{f}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item tener — the word this one is built out of.
  \item la cuchara — the one you already ask for.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{te-ne-DOR}, stress on the very end. No accent is written, because a word ending in \emph{-r} is expected to be stressed there. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el tenedor} — \textquotedblleft{}the fork.\textquotedblright{}

This one you can almost assemble from parts you own. Take \emph{tener}, to hold. Add \textbf{-dor}, the ending that names whoever or whatever does the thing. A \emph{tenedor} is \textquotedblleft{}a holder\textquotedblright{} — which is a very level-headed description of the object, once you stop seeing a fork and start seeing four prongs gripping a piece of meat.

The ending is everywhere once you look. A \emph{comedor} is where the eating is done. A \emph{mirador} is a place for looking out. English has the very same ending twice over — \textbf{-or} in \emph{inventor}, \emph{conductor}, and its plainer cousin \textbf{-er} in \emph{holder} itself — because both descend from the same Latin.

Notice what that buys you. \emph{Tenedor} is not a word to memorise; it is a word to work out, and so is the next one built the same way.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of the kitchen, and the first of them you could have predicted.

A pan is a pan and an oven is an oven. A \emph{tenedor} is a machine for holding, named by exactly that, and \emph{la cuchara} lying next to it is now the one word of the pair that has to be remembered rather than deduced.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el tenedor}
  \item \emph{la cuchara} and \emph{el tenedor}, one after the other
  \item \emph{el tenedor, por favor}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{tener} mean? (To hold, to have.) What does the ending \emph{-dor} add? (The one who does it.) So what is a \emph{tenedor}, literally? (A holder.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el ajo]{el ajo — two letters, a long history}

\label{lesson:ES-C297-ajo}



\begin{quote}
Three questions. Why does \emph{sartén} wear an accent? (Final stress, against the rule.) What is under the \emph{h} of \emph{horno}? (An \emph{f}.) And what is a \emph{tenedor}, literally? (A holder.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cebolla — what it usually goes in the pan with.
  \item la sartén — the pan in question.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{A-jo}, two beats and no more. The \emph{j} is the scrape at the back, the \emph{jota}. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el ajo} — \textquotedblleft{}the garlic.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{allium}. Three syllables have been squeezed down to two letters and a scrape, and yet the road is short: \emph{allium} to \emph{aljo} to \emph{ajo}, with the doubled \emph{l} hardening into the \emph{jota} on the way, exactly as it did in \emph{hijo} from \emph{filium}.

English kept \emph{allium} whole and handed it to the botanists, so the family that holds garlic, onions and leeks is the \textbf{allium} family on any seed packet.

The best cousin is on a menu. \textbf{Aioli} is Provençal \emph{ai} plus \emph{oli}: garlic and oil, which is the entire recipe stated in the name. Say \emph{ajo} and you are saying the first half of a sauce you already know.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of the kitchen, and the shortest word of the run carrying the longest history.

\emph{La cebolla} and \emph{el ajo} go into \emph{la sartén} together in more Spanish cooking than any two other things. You can now name the pan, the fire, the tool and half the contents.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el ajo}
  \item \emph{el ajo y la cebolla}
  \item all four — \emph{la sartén}, \emph{el horno}, \emph{el tenedor}, \emph{el ajo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What was \emph{allium}? (Garlic.) Where does English still use the whole word? (As the botanical family name.) And what two things is \emph{aioli} named after? (Garlic and oil.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la sopa]{la sopa — the bread, not the liquid}

\label{lesson:ES-C297-sopa}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: what does the ending \emph{-dor} add? (The one who does it.) What letter hides under an \emph{h}? (An \emph{f}.) And what was \emph{allium}? (Garlic.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el pan — what this word originally meant.
  \item la cuchara — what you eat it with.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{SO-pa}, stress on the first part. The \emph{s} is clean and never buzzes. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la sopa} — \textquotedblleft{}the soup.\textquotedblright{}

This one is not Latin. It came from the Germanic speakers who arrived as Rome went out, and their \textbf{suppa} did not mean the liquid at all. It meant the piece of bread you dropped into the liquid.

That is the older meal, and the honest one: broth was cheap and bread was the food. The name travelled with the bread and only later slid across to what the bread was floating in.

English has the whole family, and the same slide. A \textbf{sop} is still a bit of bread dipped in something. To \textbf{sup} is to take it, and \textbf{supper} is the meal where you did. \textbf{Soup} itself came back into English through French — the same Germanic word, one lap later.

So \emph{el pan} is not merely something you eat with \emph{la sopa}. It is what \emph{la sopa} used to be.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five: \emph{la sartén}, \emph{el horno}, \emph{el tenedor}, \emph{el ajo}, \emph{la sopa}.

A pan, a fire, a tool, a flavour and a dish — enough to describe most of what happens in a kitchen before anybody sits down. And when somebody puts it in front of you, \emph{mil gracias} is the size of thanks it deserves.

The five arrived by five different roads: a Latin pan, a Latin oven with its letter worn off, a word Spanish built for itself, a Latin plant, and a Germanic crust. That is the mix Spanish is actually made of, in one meal.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la sopa}
  \item \emph{la sopa, mil gracias}
  \item all five — \emph{la sartén}, \emph{el horno}, \emph{el tenedor}, \emph{el ajo}, \emph{la sopa}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{suppa} mean first — the bread or the broth? (The bread.) Which English meal is named from it? (\emph{Supper}.) And what is \emph{la sopa}? (The soup.)
\end{tcolorbox}
